title: Drafting Financial Services Legislation
summary: An eight-module programme helping legislative drafters and legal advisers design and draft effective, enforceable and technology-neutral financial services legislation.
intro: This training programme equips legislative drafters and government legal advisers to design and draft effective financial services legislation: choosing between principles and rules, defining the perimeter, conferring powers on regulators and building in enforcement, transition and review.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give the officials who draft and advise on financial services law a practical understanding of how legislative design choices affect regulatory outcomes, enforceability and international compliance. Participants leave able to structure primary and secondary legislation, draft workable perimeter, licensing and enforcement provisions, and keep the law technology-neutral and consistent with international standards.
sections.What It Covers: The objectives and architecture of financial services law, principles-based and rules-based drafting, primary and secondary legislation and regulator rule-making powers, defining the regulatory perimeter, licensing and authorisation provisions, supervisory and enforcement powers and sanctions, safeguards and appeals, transitional provisions, consultation and impact assessment, and technology-neutral drafting.
Intended Audience: Legislative drafters and parliamentary counsel working on financial services, payments and digital asset legislation
Legal advisers in finance ministries, central banks and other public bodies who instruct drafters or review bills
Policy officials who prepare drafting instructions and impact assessments for financial legislation
Learning Objectives: Explain how legislative design choices shape regulatory effectiveness and international compliance
Choose between principles-based and rules-based approaches and between primary and secondary legislation
Draft clear perimeter definitions, licensing provisions and exemptions
Design proportionate supervisory and enforcement powers with appropriate safeguards
Plan transitional provisions, consultation and impact assessment
Apply technology-neutral drafting techniques that keep legislation current
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as an intensive programme over two to three days or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a briefing with drafting exercises on model provisions, ending in a bill review workshop, and modules can be selected or tailored to legislation in preparation.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Experience of legislative drafting or legal advice in government is helpful. No specialist knowledge of financial services is required.
Core Reading: OECD (2012), Recommendation of the Council on Regulatory Policy and Governance
OECD (2014), The Governance of Regulators, OECD Best Practice Principles for Regulatory Policy
IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation
FSB (2014), Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes for Financial Institutions

modules.title: The Architecture of Financial Services Law
modules.summary: How financial services legislation is typically structured, the objectives it must serve, and how international standards and existing national law shape the drafter's task.
objectives: Describe the typical structure of a financial services statute
Explain how statutory objectives guide regulators and courts
Identify the international standards that legislation must reflect
syllabus: Single statutes, sectoral statutes and consolidation
Statutory objectives, principles and duties of the regulator
Translating core principles and FATF standards into national law
Interaction with company, insolvency, contract and criminal law

modules.title: Principles, Rules and Outcomes
modules.summary: The choice between principles-based, rules-based and outcomes-based drafting, and how each affects legal certainty, flexibility, enforcement and the burden on firms.
objectives: Compare principles-based, rules-based and outcomes-based approaches
Assess the effect of each on legal certainty and enforceability
Combine principles and detailed rules in a coherent framework
syllabus: Principles, rules and outcomes: strengths and weaknesses
Legal certainty, discretion and the risk of litigation
Guidance, codes and their legal status
Drafting exercise: converting a rule into a principle and back

modules.title: Primary Legislation, Secondary Legislation and Rule-Making Powers
modules.summary: What belongs in primary legislation, what can be delegated to ministers or regulators, and how to confer rule-making powers with adequate constraints and accountability.
objectives: Decide what belongs in primary and what in secondary legislation
Draft delegated and regulator rule-making powers with appropriate limits
Build in consultation, parliamentary oversight and review of rules
syllabus: Framework legislation and the limits of delegation
Ministerial regulations versus regulator rule-making
Procedural requirements: consultation, cost-benefit analysis and publication
Parliamentary scrutiny and sunset or review clauses

modules.title: Defining the Regulatory Perimeter
modules.summary: How to define regulated activities, instruments and persons so that the perimeter captures the intended risks, resists avoidance and avoids catching activity unintentionally.
objectives: Draft activity-based and entity-based perimeter definitions
Design exemptions, exclusions and territorial scope provisions
Anticipate avoidance and perimeter arbitrage
syllabus: Activity, instrument and entity definitions
By-way-of-business tests, exemptions and exclusions
Territorial scope, reverse solicitation and cross-border services
Perimeter powers to designate new activities and instruments

modules.title: Licensing and Authorisation Provisions
modules.summary: How to draft the authorisation regime: the general prohibition, threshold conditions, fit and proper tests, conditions and variations, and the powers to refuse, suspend and withdraw a licence.
objectives: Draft a general prohibition and its criminal and civil consequences
Specify threshold conditions and fitness and propriety requirements
Provide for conditions, variation, suspension and withdrawal of licences
syllabus: The general prohibition and unenforceability of agreements
Threshold conditions, controllers and change of control
Fit and proper requirements and senior manager accountability regimes
Licence conditions, variation, suspension and cancellation

modules.title: Supervisory and Enforcement Powers and Sanctions
modules.summary: The investigative, supervisory and enforcement powers regulators need, the sanctions available, and the procedural safeguards, appeals and legal protection that make them fair and durable.
objectives: Draft information-gathering, investigation and intervention powers
Design a proportionate and dissuasive sanctions framework
Provide for due process, appeals and statutory immunity
syllabus: Information requests, skilled persons, inspections and search powers
Administrative penalties, prohibition orders, restitution and criminal offences
Decision-making procedures, publication and appeals tribunals
Legal protection for the regulator and its staff

modules.title: Transitional Provisions, Consultation and Impact Assessment
modules.summary: How to move from an old regime to a new one without disruption, and how consultation and impact assessment improve legislation and its legitimacy.
objectives: Draft transitional, grandfathering and commencement provisions
Plan consultation with industry, regulators and the public
Prepare and use impact assessments and post-implementation reviews
syllabus: Commencement, staged implementation and transitional periods
Grandfathering, deemed authorisation and wind-down regimes
Consultation design and handling of responses
Regulatory impact assessment and post-implementation review

modules.title: Technology-Neutral and Future-Proof Drafting
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining how to draft for innovation such as digital assets and AI without obsolescence, and applying the programme's lessons to a draft bill.
objectives: Apply technology-neutral drafting to definitions and obligations
Assess when bespoke provisions for new technologies are justified
Review a draft bill against the principles of the programme
syllabus: Technology neutrality: principle, limits and drafting techniques
Drafting for digital assets, tokenisation and AI
Sandboxes, pilot regimes and powers to adapt
Workshop: reviewing and redrafting a financial services bill

related.title: Building a Competitive Financial Centre: Strategy, Regulation and Investment Promotion
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping ministries and investment promotion agencies build a competitive, reputable financial centre and measure the results.

related.title: Financial Crises and Public Finances: Crisis Preparedness for Government
related.summary: An eight-module advanced programme preparing finance ministries and senior officials to manage financial crises, protect public finances and coordinate resolution.

related.title: Financial Services Policy Essentials for Government
related.summary: A ten-module programme giving government officials a clear grounding in the financial system, regulatory architecture, international standards and the policy levers government holds.

related.title: Financial Services Regulation: A Briefing Programme for Parliamentarians
related.summary: A six-module, non-technical briefing programme helping parliamentarians and committee staff scrutinise financial legislation and hold regulators to account.

related.title: AI in Financial Services: Policy Choices for Government
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping policymakers understand AI in financial services and make informed choices on regulation, institutional roles and national strategy.

related.title: Developing Capital Markets and Investment Fund Industries
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping policymakers develop deep, well-regulated capital markets and fund industries through credible, well-sequenced reform.
